claims.text: The proposed starting material is a mixture of noble-metal single-source precursors, exemplified by Pt, Pd, Co, Cu, and Ni, before reduction.
Operando synchrotron X-ray techniques and real-time TEM can monitor nanoparticle formation during synthesis.
Varying temperature, precursor flow rate, and cooling rate can slow reduction kinetics and limit atom mobility.
Limited free-atom mobility increases the likelihood of stochastic random-alloy or single-phase formation in multielement nanoparticles.
Slower reduction kinetics specifically favor uniform intermixing and mitigate phase separation.
Reduction kinetics of individual precursors govern the spatial composition and whether HEA nanocrystals form homogeneous-alloy or segregated structures.
The resulting structural mediator is a homogeneous alloy with uniformly distributed metal atoms.
Defect sites in the homogeneous alloy serve as active catalytic centers.
Uniform alloying produces a more homogeneous and evenly distributed population of active sites.
Stable, evenly distributed active sites increase catalytic efficiency and durability.
Nanoparticles synthesized under reduced-mobility conditions will exhibit a single-phase HEA structure.
Nanoparticles synthesized under reduced-mobility conditions will show higher reaction rates or lower activation barriers than nanoparticles made by rapid reduction.
Rapid reduction kinetics correspond to higher precursor mobility and typically yield phase-separated or compositionally heterogeneous alloys.
Phase-separated counterparts have lower catalytic activity and durability than homogeneous, defect-rich HEA nanocrystals.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to low-temperature synthesis of noble-metal HEA nanoparticles when reaction kinetics are precisely controlled.
The proposed mechanism should apply to nitrobenzene hydrogenation or oxygen-reduction catalysis.
The quantitative relationships among precursor flow, cooling rate, alloy uniformity, and catalytic enhancement remain undetermined.
Failure of the reduced-mobility synthesis to improve both single-phase homogeneity and catalytic performance relative to the fast-reduction control would falsify the hypothesis.
